claude.sample_unit: benchmark questions (337 guideline-item, 145 management-option, 216 treatment-strategy, 80 real-case QA)
models_evaluated: DocOA (GPT-4-1106-preview with RAG and instruction prompts)

links.outcome: Accuracy of RAG-grounded DocOA versus ungrounded GPT-3.5/GPT-4 on osteoarthritis benchmark
links.effect: Overall benchmark accuracy 0.88 for DocOA vs 0.24 for GPT-4 and 0.16 for GPT-3.5 (P<.001); human-rated inaccuracy 19.3% vs 50% and 57%.
links.quote: The rate of inaccuracy was the highest for GPT-3.5 (57%, n=1200), followed by GPT-4 and DocOA at 50% (n=1200) and 19.3% (n=1200), respectively.

links.outcome: Whether RAG identifies the supporting evidence source for each answer, aiding explainability
links.effect: Authors state DocOA identifies the evidence behind answers so professionals can evaluate rationale; shown qualitatively in examples, with no quantitative test of user verification.
links.quote: When DocOA generates an OA-relevant answer, it identifies the evidence on which the answer is based and makes it clear for professionals to evaluate the rationale and accuracy of its response.

links.outcome: General LLM accuracy against current clinical guidelines for osteoarthritis management
links.effect: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 accuracy was 0.01 and 0.07 on treatment strategy QA and 0.03 and 0.01 on real-case QA; GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 were unsatisfactory on guideline-based questions.
links.quote: The accuracy of GPT-3.5 in GIQA, MOQA, TSQA, and RCQA was 0.26, 0.22, 0.01, and 0.03, respectively.

links.outcome: General LLM performance on domain-specific clinical competencies versus general medical benchmark expectations
links.effect: General LLMs had unsatisfactory performance on OA management, with marked decline as tasks shifted from knowledge to personalized treatment recommendations.
links.quote: By contrast, general-purpose models such as GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 exhibit unsatisfactory performance when benchmarked against OA management.

links.outcome: Reproducibility across 5 repeated runs and zero-shot chain-of-thought prompt variation on accuracy
links.effect: Each question was presented 5 times; chain-of-thought showed no significant improvement overall (GPT-3.5 0.16 vs 0.17, P=.41; GPT-4 0.24 vs 0.23, P=.52).
links.quote: Compared with the input-output prompt technique, no significant improvements in model performance were observed.

unlisted_practices: Combining retrieval-augmented generation with instruction prompting to create a domain-specific assistant
Building a domain-specific benchmark from clinical guidelines and real cases with physician and patient human evaluation

models_evaluated: DocOA (GPT-4-1106-preview with RAG and instruction prompts)

links.outcome: Correct retrieval of complete, relevant information
links.quote: DocOA was able to correctly recall and present complete, relevant information in 65.8% (n=1200) of the responses, followed by GPT-4 (14.3%, n=1200) and GPT-3.5 (12.0%, n=1200).

links.outcome: Clinical guideline and treatment recommendation accuracy
links.effect: GPT-4 accuracy was 0.38, 0.30, 0.07, and 0.01 for GIQA, MOQA, TSQA, and RCQA.
links.quote: The accuracy of GPT-4 in GIQA, MOQA, TSQA, and RCQA was 0.38, 0.30, 0.07, and 0.01, respectively.
GPT-3.5 presented a higher likelihood of generating harmful content (20%, n=1200) than GPT-4 (11.3%, n=1200) and DocOA (8.3%, n=1200).
The likelihoods of potentially biased content were 13.3% (n=1200), 9.5% (n=1200), and 2.8% (n=1200) for GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and DocOA, respectively.

unlisted_practices: zero-shot chain-of-thought prompting for GPT-3.5 and GPT-4

links.effect: Inaccuracy was 57% for GPT-3.5, 50% for GPT-4, and 19.3% for DocOA (n=1200).
links.quote: The rate of inaccuracy was the highest for GPT-3.5 (57%, n=1200), followed by GPT-4 and DocOA at 50% (n=1200) and 19.3% (n=1200), respectively.
